fields.h1: The Unselfishness of God by Hannah Whitall Smith: Summary & Study Guide
fields.meta_title: The Unselfishness of God by Hannah Whitall Smith: Summary & Study Guide
fields.description: Hannah Whitall Smith’s spiritual autobiography traces how she discovered that God is not stern and selfish but utterly good. A summary and study guide to The Unselfishness of God — its message, themes, and how to read it.
fields.body_html:
If you have ever suspected, somewhere beneath your prayers, that God is more concerned with His own honour than with your good, then Hannah Whitall Smith wrote The Unselfishness of God and How I Discovered It for you. It is her spiritual autobiography, published in 1903 near the end of a long and much-tested life, and its whole burden is a single discovery: that the God she had feared as a stern and self-absorbed sovereign is in truth the most generous, self-giving love in the universe. This guide walks through what the book is, how it is built, the themes at its heart, who will gain most from it, and how to read it well today. Ochorus hosts the complete text free, so you can move from this summary straight into her own words.

What the book is, and why she wrote it

The book is a testimony shaped as a life story. Smith looks back over more than seventy years and organises her spiritual history into a series of “epochs” — the awakening, the restoration of belief, the restitution of all things, and the life of faith — each one a further step into a truth she found dazzling: the unselfishness of God. She wrote it not as a system of doctrine but as a witness, so that other believers labouring under the same fears she once carried might be set free.

She opens by naming, with startling honesty, the God she grew up dreading — a deity “intent only upon His own honour and glory,” jealous of His rights and short on pity. Then she tells the reader plainly what happened.

I grew up believing God was like this. I have discovered that He is exactly the opposite. And it is of this discovery I want to tell.

Hannah Whitall Smith

That is the thesis and the method in a single breath. The book exists to trace, step by step, how a fearful searcher came to rest in the goodness of God. She anchors the aim in the prayer of Jesus in John 17:3, that eternal life is to know the only true God, and she means to show what happens to a soul when that knowledge finally lands.

How the book is structured

Smith moves in roughly chronological order, and the early chapters may surprise readers who expect a devotional treatise. She begins with her parents and her Quaker childhood, giving a warm and detailed portrait of nineteenth-century Friends — the plain bonnet, the “hat testimony,” the plainness of speech, the scruples against fiction, music, and art. This is not filler. She is showing the soil her faith grew in: a household of conscience and reform where God was real but often imagined as severe.

From that upbringing the narrative turns inward to her long spiritual searchings. She recounts the first epoch, her awakening, and then a painful stretch she calls the eclipse of faith, followed by a renewed search and the restoration of belief. Here the pace quickens into some of her best-loved chapters — the assurance of faith, the romance of the religious life, and the great turning point she titles simply “The Unselfishness of God.” The closing chapters gather the harvest: the life of faith, the way of escape, the secret of a happy life, the lovely will of God, and a final, luminous meditation on old age and death. The structure itself preaches: doubt and searching are not detours around faith but the road into it.

The central themes

The goodness and unselfishness of God. This is the sun everything else orbits. Smith had carried a “secret, torturing suspicion” that salvation was, at bottom, a selfish arrangement on God’s part. Her release came when she saw that divine love is wider than any human love she could imagine.

If I gathered together all the unselfish love of every mother’s heart in the whole world, multiplied it by millions, and pressed it into one place, I would still have nothing more than a faint shadow of the unselfishness of God.

Hannah Whitall Smith

Scripture had said as much all along — that God is love in 1 John 4:8, that He is good to all in Psalm 145:9, that He is a stronghold in Nahum 1:7, that He did not spare His own Son but gave Him for us in Romans 8:32. Smith’s gift is to make those verses feel newly true. She invites the reader to do what Psalm 34:8 commands and taste for oneself.

Assurance. A second theme is the settled confidence that one belongs to God. Smith describes being so gripped by the forgiveness of sins that she “felt like a herald marching through the corridors of a prison, with a proclamation from the King of free pardon to every prisoner.” She insists that assurance is not presumption but the plain word of God taken at face value, the promise of 1 John 5:14 that He hears us.

The rest of faith. The book’s practical centre is the message that made her famous elsewhere: the Christian’s burden is not ours to carry. She distills the whole life of holiness to surrender.

In every case, the heart of the matter was surrender — turning ourselves over to the Lord so that He might work within us, shaping both our desires and our actions according to His will.

Hannah Whitall Smith

She reduces it further to four words, “Not I, but Christ,” and calls the truth an open secret — not hidden by God but simply undiscovered by her.

It was not a secret because God hid it, but because I had not yet discovered it. It has always been an open secret — spread clearly across the pages of Scripture — if only I had possessed the spiritual perception to see it.

Hannah Whitall Smith

This is the same rest Jesus offers the weary in Matthew 11:28, the confidence that the God who began a good work will finish it in Philippians 1:6, and the freedom from sin’s dominion that Paul describes in Romans 6:6.

The lovely will of God. Flowing from all of this is a transformed view of God’s will. Once she saw His goodness, she could no longer dread what He wanted.

In the past, I had viewed God’s will as something set against me; now I discovered it was wholly for me.

Hannah Whitall Smith

Because His mercies are new every morning, as Lamentations 3:22 promises, His will becomes not a weapon but a resting place — even, at the last, in old age and death.

Who should read it

Woven through the later chapters is the story of what this discovery did to her public life. Smith does not keep the truth private; she describes how it reshaped her work, her preaching at the holiness camp meetings, and her tireless habit of pressing the good news on every friend she met. The reader watches a doctrine become a temperament — a fearful searcher turned into someone who could not stop telling others that their sins were forgiven and that they were the children of God. That movement from private relief to public joy is part of the book’s argument: a God this good cannot be kept to oneself, and the certainty of 1 John 5:1 that everyone who believes is born of God is meant to be shared.

Read this book if you are tired of a God you cannot quite trust. Smith speaks with particular tenderness to the anxious believer, the spiritual perfectionist forever “disappointed in myself,” and the doubter who fears that honest questions disqualify them. Because she narrates her own eclipse of faith without flinching, she is safe company for anyone in a season of darkness.

It is also a rich read for those drawn to Christian history and the inner life of the Quakers, and for readers who love spiritual autobiography — the tradition of Augustine’s Confessions carried into a plain-spoken American woman’s voice. Those who already know and love Smith’s The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life will find here the personal story behind that classic, the memoir that explains where the “secret” came from. And anyone facing age, loss, or bereavement will find a companion who buried four children and a shaken marriage and still called death “a delicious prospect.”

How to read it today

A few suggestions will help the book give up its treasure. First, do not skip the Quaker chapters. They read like memoir rather than devotion, but they are where Smith shows the fearful picture of God she inherited, and the release lands harder when you have felt the weight it lifts. Second, read it as a story with a destination. Watch the four epochs build; the point is cumulative, and the payoff in the chapter “The Unselfishness of God” means more if you have travelled the searching that precedes it.

Third, keep a Bible open beside her. Smith reasons constantly from Scripture, and testing her claims against passages like John 17:3, 1 John 4:8, and Romans 8:32 turns reading into prayer. Fourth, resist the impulse to argue with her wider hopes about God’s dealings and stay with her central discovery, which is thoroughly biblical: that God is good, and that God is enough. Finally, read slowly and personally. This is a book of first-person testimony; the honest response is to ask where your own picture of God is more fearful than the truth. When you finish, her companion volume The God of All Comfort presses the same tender vision further, and the life of Hannah Whitall Smith herself fills in the griefs she met with this faith.

For reflection

Sit with these questions, alone or in a group, and let them draw you back into the text:

  1. Smith confesses she long imagined God as “one of the most selfish, self-absorbed beings in the universe.” In what specific ways does your own working picture of God differ from the good and generous Father she describes?
  2. She calls the rest of faith “an open secret” that God never hid. What has kept you from laying down a burden you were never meant to carry?
  3. Read Matthew 11:28 and Philippians 1:6 slowly. Where are you still trying to do God’s work of transforming yourself, rather than trusting Him to finish what He began?
  4. Smith came to see God’s will as “wholly for me.” Is there a circumstance in your life you are treating as God’s severity that might, in His hands, be His kindness?
  5. She met the loss of four children and a broken marriage with a faith that only brightened. What would it mean for you to build assurance on the fact of God’s love rather than your feelings about it?

Whatever answers come, Smith would point you past herself to the discovery that steadied her whole life — that God is, that God is good, and that God is enough. You can read every word of her testimony free on Ochorus and see for yourself.
